note: For weeks Billy rides the mountain country with his packhorse, asking anyone who will answer what became of his brother.
credit: Horse and rider traced from Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain), and the same horse with the rider cut away and a pack drawn on; the pines as in the Madera fair drawing
reasoning: A character vignette halfway along the J7 leg from Namiquipa to Temósachic (j7-seg-31, 50% along). The ref is Namiquipa, the leg's start, because Temósachic carries the corridero.

name: The brick store at Colonia Morelos
stands_for: Colonia Morelos, the old Mormon settlement where the wolf is shown at the fair (J2)
note: Riding into Colonia Morelos in search of the wolf, Billy passes the brick houses and tin roofs of a Mormon settlement of the last century, and a store of brick behind a wooden false front, with bunting hung in the trees across from it.
credit: Drawn from the book's description; the false front and brick courses after 1930s Historic American Buildings Survey photographs of false-front stores (public domain)
reasoning: Design section 10's brick Mormon storehouse. The book's building at Colonia Morelos is a brick store behind a board false front, so that is what is drawn. It stands at the fair's stop, which also carries the wolf's cart, with the cockpit drawing at the hacienda close by. It has no caption: on every side a caption would run into one of those two drawings. The drawing at Colonia Juárez shows that colony's houses and orchards, not a store.

name: The old man's oxen at the river
stands_for: The crossing of the old wagon road to Namiquipa (J4)
note: While the horses drink at the old wagon road's river crossing, Billy watches an old farmer dressed in white field clothes drive a yoked pair of oxen down from the far bank to drink. The two talk of crops and weather.
label: Oxen at the river
credit: Drawn; the oxen are the corriente steers of this set made heavier (after photographs by Carol M. Highsmith, public domain, and Clinton and Charles Robertson, CC BY 2.0), the yoke and the farmer after C. B. Waite's photographs of ox teams in Mexico, 1900s (public domain)
reasoning: Design section 10 lists an ox cart in the Bavispe valley. The book has no ox cart there: its oxen are this yoked pair, with no cart, at the crossing of the old wagon road to Namiquipa, so the drawing shows them wading in to drink.

name: Herefords of the Babícora
stands_for: The Babícora ranch's whitefaced cattle on the high grassland (J7)
note: Riding the high grassland of the Babícora for days, Billy sometimes sees parties of the ranch's vaqueros crossing it on mules or driving cattle. They take a nickname from the whitefaced Hereford cattle the ranch breeds.
label: Hereford whitefaces, Babícora
credit: Drawn after 1930s US Department of Agriculture photographs of Hereford cattle (public domain)
reasoning: Design section 10's Babícora Hereford. The book names no breed, but the white-faced cattle the Babícora raised were Herefords. The book names them where Billy spends days riding the Babícora uplands, so the drawing stands at that stop.

name: The she-wolf's mate in the trap
stands_for: Where the she-wolf left her mate, in the Sonoran mountains (J1)
note: Two weeks before she crosses into New Mexico, the she-wolf's mate is caught by a forefoot in a steel trap somewhere in the Sonoran mountains. He bares his teeth to send her away, but she lies flat just out of the chain's reach and stays.
label: Her mate in the trap
credit: Drawn after the wolf and trap photographs in Vernon Bailey's US Department of Agriculture bulletins on wolves, 1907 to the 1910s (public domain); the wolves are the traced she-wolf (US Fish and Wildlife Service photograph, public domain)
reasoning: The book places the trap only somewhere in the Sonoran mountains, two weeks before her journey north, so the drawing stands near the start of her first leg, the way she would have come. The wolves fill the drawing and the trap is small, so it does not repeat the steel trap drawn for Billy's trapline.

name: The Model A and the trapped wolf
stands_for: Billy bringing the trapped she-wolf to the road (J2)
note: Billy has hauled the gagged wolf up onto the road when an old rancher drives up over the rise in his Model A pickup. Billy pulls her into the ditch beside the fence and lies holding her, his arms round her neck, as the truck stops alongside.
label: The rancher's Model A
credit: Drawn after photographs of the Ford Model A pickup, 1928 to 1931; the wolf is the traced she-wolf (US Fish and Wildlife Service photograph, public domain)
reasoning: Billy meets the rancher on the road just past the trap site on Cloverdale Creek, so the drawing stands on the leg from Cloverdale Creek road towards Robertson's crossfence. From zoom 10, as the drawings of the she-wolf and the cholla and of Billy and the dog are close by.

name: The bearers and their dead companion
stands_for: The mine labourers Billy eats with on the trail down to the Bavispe (J2)
note: Below the trail Billy comes on six mine labourers taking the body of a companion, killed at his work, home across the mountains to their village. It lies apart on a litter of poles and hide, wrapped in tied canvas under green branches, and the men share their meal with him.
label: The bearers' noon halt
credit: Drawn after Carl Lumholtz's photographs in Unknown Mexico, 1902 (public domain)
reasoning: They have stopped for their noon meal just after Billy comes through a gap and first sees the Bavispe valley, so the drawing stands near the start of the leg from the passes of the Sierra de la Cabellera towards the river. The note does not name the men's people, and the drawing shows only what the book gives: the litter, the canvas and the tumpline.

name: Billy's horse in the storm
stands_for: The hailstorm on the road north towards Ojito (J3)
note: Riding north from Morelos into low broken hills, Billy is caught by hail and shelters in a ruined group of buildings beside the road. That night, through gaps in the walls, he can see his horse out by the road, lit by flashes of lightning.
label: Sheltering from the hail
credit: Drawn after Farm Security Administration and Historic American Buildings Survey photographs of ruined adobes, 1930s (public domain); the horse is the traced Muybridge horse with the rider cut away, Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain)
reasoning: The storm overtakes him after his last crossing of the river, early on the road from Morelos north towards Ojito, so the drawing stands about a third along that leg. The book gives no place for the ruins.

name: Names cut in the rock of the pass
stands_for: The Guadalupe pass on Billy's ride home from Douglas (J3)
note: Riding home over the Guadalupes on a cold evening, Billy reads old names and dates cut in the rock of the pass by travellers long dead.
label: Old names in the rock
credit: Drawn after 1930s National Park Service and Historic American Buildings Survey photographs of Inscription Rock, El Morro, New Mexico (public domain); the rider traced from Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain), mirrored
reasoning: The names are in the pass itself, where the leg from the border at Douglas ends, so the drawing stands just short of the pass. The book gives none of the names: the date in the drawing is invented. From zoom 10, as the bootheel is crowded further out.

name: A rider across the playa
stands_for: The brothers' camp on the flats west of Lordsburg (J4)
note: At sunrise the brothers watch a lone rider come towards them across the playa's grey clay, seen first as a wavering reflection on the shallow water.
label: Rider on the playa
credit: Horse and rider traced from Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain), with his reflection; the playa after Erwin E. Smith's photographs of cowboys, 1905 to 1915, and Russell Lee's Farm Security Administration photographs, 1939 to 1940 (public domain)
reasoning: The rider comes across the flats at sunrise to the brothers' camp, so the drawing stands at the very start of the leg from the camp towards the San Simon, out on the playa.

name: The miners' family at the old silver mine
stands_for: The brothers' ride across the sierra east of Bacerac (J4)
note: One evening, across a valley, the brothers see the spoil heaps of a worked-out silver mine. A family of wandering miners camped there in huts of woven sticks, among the rusted machinery, stand in a line by their fire, tallest to smallest, hands raised against the sun to watch them go by.
label: The old silver mine
credit: Drawn after photographs of mines and mining camps in the Sierra Madre of Sonora and Chihuahua, 1900s to 1930s (public domain)
reasoning: The mine comes after two days' riding in the sierra beyond Bacerac, on the way to the eastern rim, so the drawing stands halfway along that leg. The book gives no name or place for it.

name: The horned moon over the night ride
stands_for: The brothers' night ride west from the Boquilla road to a dry camp (J4)
note: Driving their horses upcountry all night, keeping off the river, the brothers ride under a thin crescent moon low in the western sky, horns upward, with Venus shining just above it.
label: The horned moon, Venus above
credit: Drawn after Frederic Remington's night pieces and almanac woodcuts of the moon (public domain); the horses traced from Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain)
reasoning: The moon is seen as the night ride sets out, and the ride follows the leg from the Boquilla road west to the dry camp, so the drawing stands halfway along it. The moon is drawn as the book gives it: a thin crescent, horns up, and Venus straight above.

name: Riders going to the Saturday dance
stands_for: Billy's ride from La Boquilla to La Pinta (J5)
note: Riding south towards dark, Billy meets boys and young men riding north to a Saturday dance on burros and small mine mules, in polished boots and pressed cotton shirts, their hair combed flat.
label: Off to the Saturday dance
credit: Horse and rider traced from Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain), with a mule's ears and no hat; the dress after Hugo Brehme's photographs of rural Mexico, 1910s to 1930s
reasoning: He meets the riders between La Boquilla and La Pinta towards dark, so the drawing stands halfway along that leg.

name: “The girl” in a blue dress
stands_for: “The girl” riding past the stream of the Santa María headwaters (J5)
note: Waking late beside a stream below the road, Billy sees “the girl” ride by in a new blue cotton dress and a little straw hat trailing a green ribbon, and saddles his horse to follow her.
label: “The girl” in her blue dress
credit: Horse and rider traced from Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain); the dress, hat and ribbon after the Casasola archive's and Hugo Brehme's photographs of rancheras, 1910s to 1930s
reasoning: Billy wakes by a stream an hour west of Santa Ana de Babícora and she passes on the road soon after, so the drawing stands near the start of the leg from that stream to Santa Ana. Two inks cannot show her blue, so the label gives it. From zoom 10, as the Babícora roads are crowded further out.

name: The night bus north past Socorro
stands_for: Billy's bus ride to try the recruiting office at Albuquerque (J7)
note: Riding the bus north to try the army once more, Billy watches at nightfall beyond Socorro as flights of waterfowl circle down to the marshes along the river, though he cannot hear them over the bus.
label: Night bus past Socorro
credit: Drawn after photographs of the Yellow Coach model 743 Silversides coach, 1940
reasoning: Night falls a little past Socorro, where the leg from Deming ends, so the drawing stands there. The book names no bus company: the coach is drawn as the Silversides that Greyhound bought in numbers from 1940.

name: The gold star in a ranch house window
stands_for: Billy's war years on the ranches, and his ride south from Magdalena (J7)
note: Billy drifts from ranch to ranch through the war years. By the third spring of it, nearly every ranch house in that country has a service flag with a gold star hung in a window, for a son the war has killed.
label: Gold star, ranch house window
credit: Drawn after the service flag as specified in 1942 and Office of War Information photographs of service flags in windows (public domain)
reasoning: The book gives the gold stars to the whole country Billy works in, not to one house, and then has him ride south from a small ranch near Magdalena to cross the last highway east of Steins, so the drawing stands halfway along that leg.

name: Children on Niño at the stream
stands_for: The morning Billy leaves Janos for Casas Grandes (J7)
note: Waking sick in an empty house after a night of drinking, Billy walks his horses down to a stream below the town and sets three children up on Niño, one behind another, the eldest holding the two little ones.
label: Children up on Niño
credit: Horse traced from Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain), with the rider cut away; the children after Russell Lee's Farm Security Administration photographs, 1939 to 1940 (public domain)
reasoning: The stream crosses the road just south of town, the day Billy leaves for Casas Grandes, so the drawing stands at the start of the leg from Janos.

name: The wedding carreta at Namiquipa
stands_for: The wedding party on the road into Namiquipa (J7)
note: Riding into Namiquipa at first light, Billy meets a wedding party on the road: a plain wooden cart decked with bunting, a cotton sheet on a frame of willow hoops to keep off the sun, one small grey mule, and the bride alone under her parasol.
label: Wedding carreta, Namiquipa
credit: Drawn after C. B. Waite's photographs of carretas in Mexico, 1900s (public domain); the mule is the traced Muybridge horse with the rider cut away and a mule's ears, Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion plate 580, 1887 (public domain)
reasoning: He meets the party as he comes into Namiquipa, where the leg from Santa Ana de Babícora ends, so the drawing stands just short of Namiquipa. The cart is drawn with the book's canopy, bunting and one mule, unlike the oxen at the river or the gypsies' float.
